screens.title: Security Groups: instance-level, stateful firewalls
screens.narratorSegment: Security Groups are the primary instance-level firewall in AWS and they are stateful. That means when you allow outbound traffic from an instance, return traffic is automatically permitted even if no separate inbound rule exists. This simplifies rule sets: you open only necessary ports and trust the stateful connection returns will be handled. A concrete example is a web server behind an Application Load Balancer. The SG for the web server allows inbound traffic on port 8080 only from the ALBs Security Group, and it allows outbound traffic to a database port in a separate database SG. The practical benefit is least privilege: the web server has exactly the network paths it needs and no others. A frequent misconception is that Security Groups can explicitly deny traffic; they cannot. They only allow. If a connection is not allowed by any rule, it is implicitly denied. Another important detail: Security Groups can be attached to other resources besides EC2, like RDS, ENIs for Lambda and network interfaces created by load balancers. This lets you build predictable, group-based access patterns. When designing rules, choose narrow CIDR ranges or referenced Security Groups over broad ranges. As a final takeaway, treat Security Groups as the first line of defense for instances and prefer referencing SGs for internal communication rather than using wide IP ranges.

keyIdea.title: Security Groups are stateful
keyIdea.text: They allow return traffic automatically and only support allow rules; use them to enforce least privilege at the instance level.

content.html:
Core Concept › Security Groups
Security Groups: stateful, instance-level
They control inbound and outbound traffic for EC2, RDS, ALB ENIs, and Lambda ENIs using allow-only rules and automatic return traffic handling.
Behavior
  • Stateful: return traffic is permitted automatically.
  • Allow-only rules; no explicit DENY.
  • Attach to instances and network interfaces.
Key takeaway
Use Security Groups to enforce least privilege at the resource level and prefer SG references for internal communication.
Concrete example
Web tier: ALB listens on 443 with an ACM cert. ALBs SG allows client HTTPS. Web servers SG allows inbound 8080 only from ALBs SG. Database SG allows port 3306 only from web server SG.
Common mistake
Leaving SSH open to 0.0.0.0/0 exposes instances to brute-force attacks; instead restrict SSH to your IP or use a bastion host.
Check
When traffic is blocked, confirm the instance SG allows the connection and that no other SG is denying it implicitly by omission.

screens.title: Authoring Security Group rules safely
screens.narratorSegment: Writing Security Group rules is a deliberate design decision, not a checklist item. The guiding rule is least privilege: open only the ports and CIDR ranges your application needs. A simple pattern is to allow HTTP and HTTPS from the public internet to a load balancer but restrict SSH to a specific administrator IP. Another powerful pattern is SG referencing, where you allow traffic from another Security Group rather than from an IP range. For example, allow port 8080 from the ALBs Security Group ID; this ensures only the load balancer can reach the web servers. This avoids brittle IP-based rules and simplifies scaling because new ALB instances inherit the same SG. A frequent misconception is to assume outbound rules are less important; overly permissive outbound rules can let compromised instances communicate freely. When possible, restrict outbound traffic to known service endpoints or to the database ports used internally. Also consider using ephemeral port ranges in NACLs for return traffic when you need stateless controls. Practically, document why each rule exists, set descriptive tags, and automate rule creation through infrastructure-as-code so review and rollback are straightforward. A final quick check: confirm both the Security Group and the subnet NACL allow the same traffic path when troubleshooting reachability.

content.html:
Best Practice › Authoring Security Group rules
Rule-writing process
1
Identify minimal ports
Open only what the service requires, e.g., 80/443 for HTTP/HTTPS, and specific DB ports for backend.
2
Prefer SG references
Allow the ALBs Security Group rather than 0.0.0.0/0 to restrict internal traffic paths.
3
Restrict outbound
Limit outbound to services and ports your app needs; avoid broad 0.0.0.0/0 egress unless required.
Scenario
You have an ALB and three web servers. Create an ALB SG allowing HTTPS from 0.0.0.0/0. Web servers SG allows 8080 only from ALB SG and database SG allows 3306 only from web server SG.
Check your assumptions
  • Is SSH limited to admin IPs or a bastion host?
  • Are outbound rules narrower than 0.0.0.0/0 where possible?
  • Are SG rules managed via IaC for auditability?

screens.title: Network ACLs (NACLs): subnet-level, stateless controls
screens.narratorSegment: Network Access Control Lists are stateless firewalls applied to subnets. Unlike Security Groups, NACLs require you to explicitly allow both the initial traffic and the return traffic, because they do not track connection state. NACLs evaluate rules in ascending order and the first rule that matches the packet is applied. A NACL can contain both ALLOW and DENY rules, which makes it useful for denying entire CIDR ranges at the subnet boundary. A concrete use case is blocking a known malicious IP block from reaching any instance in the subnet: apply a DENY rule early in the rule list. Because NACLs are stateless, if you allow inbound port 80, you must also allow ephemeral outbound ports for the return path. A common misconception is to rely solely on NACLs for fine-grained access; they are coarser by design. Security Groups are usually the day-to-day tool for developers because they are stateful and attached directly to resources. Reserve NACLs for edge-level protections and quick deny rules that apply to entire subnets. When troubleshooting, remember to check both the NACL and the Security Group: either can silently block traffic.

keyIdea.text: Use them for subnet-wide allows or denies; remember to add return rules since they don't track connection state.

content.html:
Definition › Network ACLs (NACLs)
What NACLs do
  • Applied to subnets to allow or deny traffic entering or leaving all instances in the subnet.
  • Stateless: must permit both directions explicitly.
  • Rules are evaluated in numeric order; first match wins.
Practical note
Use DENY entries to block malicious IP ranges for an entire subnet. Use ALLOW entries for required ports and remember to add corresponding return rules.
Example rule order
Rule 100: DENY 203.0.113.0/24. Rule 200: ALLOW TCP 80 from 0.0.0.0/0. Rule 300: ALLOW ephemeral ports for return 1024-65535.

screens.title: Security Groups vs NACLs
screens.narratorSegment: Both Security Groups and NACLs are firewalls, but they serve different roles. Security Groups are stateful and applied to individual resources; they are the go-to tool for developers because they are easier to reason about and scale as resources spin up and down. NACLs are stateless and applied to subnets; they are useful for broad, ordered allow or deny rules that affect all instances in a subnet. A practical example helps: to block a malicious IP across an entire subnet, a NACL deny is efficient. To ensure only a load balancer can reach web servers, a Security Group reference is ideal. Misunderstandings often arise around rule precedence: Security Groups do not have ordered rules and cannot deny; they only allow. NACLs evaluate rules in order and can deny. When troubleshooting connectivity problems, check both: a permissive Security Group cannot override a NACL deny. Also remember the return-traffic difference: with Security Groups you don't need a matching return rule; with NACLs you do. Choose Security Groups for most application-level rules and reserve NACLs for subnet-scoped, often security-operations driven controls. Security Groups vs NACLs means use sgs for resource-specific, stateful access; use nacls for broad, ordered subnet-level allows and denies.. In practical terms, when to use instance-level stateful rules or subnet-level stateless filters. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Comparison › Security Groups vs NACLs
Security Groups
  • Instance-level, stateful; attach to ENIs.
  • Allow-only rules; no explicit deny.
  • Best for application-level access control and internal SG references.
Network ACLs
  • Subnet-level, stateless; rules processed in order.
  • Support ALLOW and DENY entries; good for blocking CIDR ranges.
  • Use for perimeter controls and quick subnet-wide denies.
Troubleshooting checklist
Check SG inbound rules
Check NACL rule order
Confirm return path is allowed

screens.title: VPC Endpoints: private connectivity to AWS services
screens.narratorSegment: VPC Endpoints enable private connections between your VPC and supported AWS services without traversal of the public internet. There are two main types: Interface Endpoints and Gateway Endpoints. Interface Endpoints create an Elastic Network Interface with a private IP address in your subnet and are powered by AWS PrivateLink. They are commonly used for services that require an ENI, like SQS, SNS, KMS, and many partner services. Gateway Endpoints, on the other hand, are used specifically for S3 and DynamoDB. A gateway endpoint becomes a target for a route in your route table so traffic to the supported service is routed through the gateway. The practical benefit is reducing the attack surface and avoiding NAT or Internet Gateways for simple service access from private subnets. A typical developer scenario is an EC2 instance in a private subnet that needs to list S3 buckets: with a Gateway Endpoint for S3, the instance can reach S3 without a NAT. Remember to update route tables for gateway endpoints and to create interface endpoints in the right subnets and security groups when your service supports PrivateLink.

keyIdea.title: Endpoints keep traffic private
keyIdea.text: Use interface endpoints for PrivateLink services and gateway endpoints for S3/DynamoDB to avoid public internet routing.

content.html:
Core Concept › VPC Endpoints
Why use endpoints?
They keep traffic on the AWS network, reduce reliance on NAT/IGW, and shrink your public attack surface while simplifying costs and routing.
Interface Endpoint: ENI in subnet, PrivateLink, used for many AWS and partner services.
Gateway Endpoint: Route table target for S3 and DynamoDB.
Concrete example
An application in a private subnet needs to write to S3. Instead of creating a NAT Gateway, add a Gateway VPC Endpoint for S3 and update the private subnet route table to direct S3 traffic to the endpoint. The instance can now communicate with S3 privately.
Checklist
Confirm route table entries for gateway endpoints and security group references for interface endpoints. Verify from an instance using aws s3 ls or equivalent calls.

screens.title: Interface vs Gateway Endpoints
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing between interface and gateway endpoints depends on the service. Gateway endpoints are available only for S3 and DynamoDB; they integrate with route tables and require no ENI. They are ideal when many private instances need scalable, simple access to those services without modifying each instances network interface. Interface endpoints create ENIs in specific subnets and are powered by PrivateLink; use them for services like SQS, SNS, KMS, and many partner services. An important practical consideration is security group attachment: interface endpoints have SGs that control which subnets and instances can reach the endpoint. One misconception is assuming every AWS service can use a gateway endpoint; many cannot and require interface endpoints or other network arrangements. Another operational detail: gateway endpoints change route tables, so if you have multiple private route tables, ensure you update each one that must route to S3 or DynamoDB. Interface endpoints can incur costs associated with ENI-based PrivateLink usage; gateway endpoints do not use ENIs. When designing your architecture, map the services your application uses to endpoint types to decide whether you need route table changes or security group rules for endpoint ENIs.

keyIdea.title: Pick endpoint by service
keyIdea.text: Use gateway endpoints for S3/DynamoDB; use interface endpoints for PrivateLink services that require ENIs and SG control.

content.html:
Deep Dive › Interface vs Gateway Endpoints
Gateway Endpoint
Target for route tables. Supports S3 and DynamoDB. No ENI required. Simple and efficient for subnet-wide access.
Interface Endpoint
Creates ENIs, powered by PrivateLink. Use for SQS, SNS, KMS, SSM, and many other services. Attach Security Groups to control access.
Design notes
Map your services to endpoint types, update route tables for gateway endpoints, and attach tight security groups to interface endpoints to enforce least privilege.

screens.title: Creating a Gateway VPC Endpoint for S3
screens.narratorSegment: Creating a Gateway VPC Endpoint for S3 is a straightforward way to let private subnets reach S3 without a NAT Gateway or Internet Gateway. The process is: identify the VPC ID and the route table IDs for private subnets, create the gateway endpoint specifying those route tables, and then verify that the route table has an entry directing S3 traffic to the endpoint. A concrete example is an EC2 instance in a private subnet that cannot reach S3 until you add this endpoint. After creation, run aws s3 ls from the instance to verify you can list buckets. Be careful: if your subnet uses multiple route tables, you must add the endpoint routes to each relevant table. A common misconception is that endpoints automatically adjust security groups. Gateway endpoints do not rely on ENIs, so they do not attach security groups; interface endpoints do. For auditing, tag the endpoint with purpose and owner details. Finally, after testing successful access, remove any temporary public IPs used for initial SSH access to the instance so the subnet remains truly private. Creating a Gateway VPC Endpoint for S3 means create endpoint, associate route tables, verify route entry, and test s3 access from a private instance with aws s3 ls.. In practical terms, route table changes and a private s3 access workflow. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Finally, after testing successful access, remove any temporary public IPs used for initial SSH access to the instance so the subnet remains truly private. Process Flow › Gateway VPC Endpoint for S3
Step-by-step

screens.title: AWS Certificate Manager and TLS termination
screens.narratorSegment: Securing client connections requires SSL/TLS certificates, and AWS Certificate Manager simplifies issuing and rotating those certificates. With ACM you request a public certificate and validate domain ownership via DNS or email. Once issued, you attach the ACM certificate to an Application Load Balancer listener configured for HTTPS. The ALB then performs TLS termination: it decrypts the client traffic and forwards plain HTTP to backend instances if desired. This has two practical benefits: you centralize certificate management and avoid manual renewal on each backend, and you simplify backend configurations by handling encryption at the edge. A common misconception is that backends must always use HTTPS; in many architectures you intentionally terminate TLS at the ALB and rely on SGs in private subnets to protect internal traffic. If you require end-to-end encryption, you can install certificates on backend instances as well and configure ALB to use HTTPS to targets. Remember to use the ACM certificate ARN when associating with the ALB listener and validate domain ownership during the request process. The final takeaway: ACM reduces operational burden and lowers the risk of expired certificates disrupting client traffic.

keyIdea.title: CLI pattern
keyIdea.text: Create SG, add ingress rules, create gateway endpoint with route table IDs, then verify S3 access from a private instance.

content.html:
Live CLI Demo › Create SG and Gateway Endpoint
Example commands

# Create a Security Group for a web server
aws ec2 create-security-group --group-name WebServerSG --description 'Web Server Security Group' --vpc-id vpc-0abcdef1234567890

# Save the SG ID returned by the command
SG_ID="sg-0abcdef1234567890"

# Allow inbound HTTP (port 80) from anywhere
aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress --group-id $SG_ID --protocol tcp --port 80 --cidr 0.0.0.0/0

# Allow inbound HTTPS (port 443) from anywhere
aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress --group-id $SG_ID --protocol tcp --port 443 --cidr 0.0.0.0/0

# Allow inbound SSH (port 22) from YOUR_IP_ADDRESS only
aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress --group-id $SG_ID --protocol tcp --port 22 --cidr YOUR_IP_ADDRESS/32

# Create a Gateway VPC Endpoint for S3
VPC_ID="vpc-0abcdef1234567890"
ROUTE_TABLE_ID_1="rtb-0abcdef1234567890"
aws ec2 create-vpc-endpoint --vpc-id $VPC_ID --service-name com.amazonaws.us-east-1.s3 --vpc-endpoint-type Gateway --route-table-ids $ROUTE_TABLE_ID_1

# After creation, verify from your instance:
# aws s3 ls
Verification steps
  1. From private instance, run: aws s3 ls — expect failure without endpoint or NAT.
  2. Create gateway endpoint and associate route tables.
  3. Run aws s3 ls again — expect success when correctly configured.
Warning
Replace placeholder IDs and your IP before running commands. Leaving SSH open to the world is unsafe.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson well build a mental model for the layers of network defense available inside an Amazon VPC. Youll learn why Security Groups act as instance-level, stateful firewalls while Network Access Control Lists operate at the subnet level and are stateless. Well also explain how VPC Endpoints let your private resources reach AWS services without touching the public internet, and how AWS Certificate Manager simplifies SSL/TLS for secure client connections. Understanding these elements together helps you design least-privilege, resilient network controls for web applications. For example, you will see a common pattern: an Application Load Balancer terminates TLS using an ACM certificate, then forwards decrypted traffic to EC2 instances protected by Security Groups that only allow traffic from the load balancer. Well cover practical mistakes to avoid, like exposing SSH to the world, and walk through commands to create a Security Group and an S3 Gateway endpoint. By the end youll be able to choose between SGs and NACLs, configure private service access with endpoints, and deploy TLS with ACM. Think about your current apps: where can you reduce public exposure while keeping necessary routes open?

By the end of this chapter you will be able to configure and reason about the primary network controls inside an Amazon VPC. First, you will understand how Security Groups act as stateful, instance-level firewalls and how to author rules that enforce least privilege for your EC2 instances and other resources. Second, you will be able to contrast Security Groups with Network ACLs, describing when a subnet-level, stateless deny rule is appropriate. Third, you will implement VPC Endpoints to enable private access to supported AWS services without routing traffic over the public internet. Finally, you will use AWS Certificate Manager to provision and attach SSL/TLS certificates to an Application Load Balancer so client connections remain encrypted. Each objective is practical: you will write rules, create endpoints, and attach certificates, and you will also know common pitfalls to avoid. For instance, you will learn why opening SSH to 0.0.0.0/0 is risky, and how to instead restrict SSH to a trusted IP or a bastion host. These skills are essential for deploying secure, private, and operationally simple cloud applications.

These objectives translate directly into tasks you will perform when deploying and securing services. You will create Security Groups and attach them to EC2 or load balancer interfaces. You will practice using referenced Security Group rules so internal services communicate without opening public ports. You will also create and inspect NACL entries, observing how rule order and explicit deny entries change traffic flow. For private AWS service access, you will create both interface and gateway VPC Endpoints, verify route table entries for gateway endpoints to S3 or DynamoDB, and test private connectivity from an instance in a private subnet. Finally, you will request an ACM certificate, validate ownership, and associate the certificate with an Application Load Balancer listener to enable HTTPS for your application. Throughout, youll learn to check both security group rules and the subnet NACL when a port appears blocked, and to prefer private endpoints and managed TLS to reduce public exposure. These skills reduce operational risk and simplify compliance checks for secure cloud applications.

Security Groups are the primary instance-level firewall in AWS and they are stateful. That means when you allow outbound traffic from an instance, return traffic is automatically permitted even if no separate inbound rule exists. This simplifies rule sets: you open only necessary ports and trust the stateful connection returns will be handled. A concrete example is a web server behind an Application Load Balancer. The SG for the web server allows inbound traffic on port 8080 only from the ALBs Security Group, and it allows outbound traffic to a database port in a separate database SG. The practical benefit is least privilege: the web server has exactly the network paths it needs and no others. A frequent misconception is that Security Groups can explicitly deny traffic; they cannot. They only allow. If a connection is not allowed by any rule, it is implicitly denied. Another important detail: Security Groups can be attached to other resources besides EC2, like RDS, ENIs for Lambda and network interfaces created by load balancers. This lets you build predictable, group-based access patterns. When designing rules, choose narrow CIDR ranges or referenced Security Groups over broad ranges. As a final takeaway, treat Security Groups as the first line of defense for instances and prefer referencing SGs for internal communication rather than using wide IP ranges.

Writing Security Group rules is a deliberate design decision, not a checklist item. The guiding rule is least privilege: open only the ports and CIDR ranges your application needs. A simple pattern is to allow HTTP and HTTPS from the public internet to a load balancer but restrict SSH to a specific administrator IP. Another powerful pattern is SG referencing, where you allow traffic from another Security Group rather than from an IP range. For example, allow port 8080 from the ALBs Security Group ID; this ensures only the load balancer can reach the web servers. This avoids brittle IP-based rules and simplifies scaling because new ALB instances inherit the same SG. A frequent misconception is to assume outbound rules are less important; overly permissive outbound rules can let compromised instances communicate freely. When possible, restrict outbound traffic to known service endpoints or to the database ports used internally. Also consider using ephemeral port ranges in NACLs for return traffic when you need stateless controls. Practically, document why each rule exists, set descriptive tags, and automate rule creation through infrastructure-as-code so review and rollback are straightforward. A final quick check: confirm both the Security Group and the subnet NACL allow the same traffic path when troubleshooting reachability.

Network Access Control Lists are stateless firewalls applied to subnets. Unlike Security Groups, NACLs require you to explicitly allow both the initial traffic and the return traffic, because they do not track connection state. NACLs evaluate rules in ascending order and the first rule that matches the packet is applied. A NACL can contain both ALLOW and DENY rules, which makes it useful for denying entire CIDR ranges at the subnet boundary. A concrete use case is blocking a known malicious IP block from reaching any instance in the subnet: apply a DENY rule early in the rule list. Because NACLs are stateless, if you allow inbound port 80, you must also allow ephemeral outbound ports for the return path. A common misconception is to rely solely on NACLs for fine-grained access; they are coarser by design. Security Groups are usually the day-to-day tool for developers because they are stateful and attached directly to resources. Reserve NACLs for edge-level protections and quick deny rules that apply to entire subnets. When troubleshooting, remember to check both the NACL and the Security Group: either can silently block traffic.

Both Security Groups and NACLs are firewalls, but they serve different roles. Security Groups are stateful and applied to individual resources; they are the go-to tool for developers because they are easier to reason about and scale as resources spin up and down. NACLs are stateless and applied to subnets; they are useful for broad, ordered allow or deny rules that affect all instances in a subnet. A practical example helps: to block a malicious IP across an entire subnet, a NACL deny is efficient. To ensure only a load balancer can reach web servers, a Security Group reference is ideal. Misunderstandings often arise around rule precedence: Security Groups do not have ordered rules and cannot deny; they only allow. NACLs evaluate rules in order and can deny. When troubleshooting connectivity problems, check both: a permissive Security Group cannot override a NACL deny. Also remember the return-traffic difference: with Security Groups you don't need a matching return rule; with NACLs you do. Choose Security Groups for most application-level rules and reserve NACLs for subnet-scoped, often security-operations driven controls. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

VPC Endpoints enable private connections between your VPC and supported AWS services without traversal of the public internet. There are two main types: Interface Endpoints and Gateway Endpoints. Interface Endpoints create an Elastic Network Interface with a private IP address in your subnet and are powered by AWS PrivateLink. They are commonly used for services that require an ENI, like SQS, SNS, KMS, and many partner services. Gateway Endpoints, on the other hand, are used specifically for S3 and DynamoDB. A gateway endpoint becomes a target for a route in your route table so traffic to the supported service is routed through the gateway. A typical developer scenario is an EC2 instance in a private subnet that needs to list S3 buckets: with a Gateway Endpoint for S3, the instance can reach S3 without a NAT. Remember to update route tables for gateway endpoints and to create interface endpoints in the right subnets and security groups when your service supports PrivateLink.

They are ideal when many private instances need scalable, simple access to those services without modifying each instances network interface. Interface endpoints create ENIs in specific subnets and are powered by PrivateLink; use them for services like SQS, SNS, KMS, and many partner services. An important practical consideration is security group attachment: interface endpoints have SGs that control which subnets and instances can reach the endpoint. First, Security Groups are stateful and allow return traffic automatically, so use them to define per-resource access and prefer SG references for internal communication. Second, NACLs are stateless and processed in order; use DENY entries to block CIDR ranges at the subnet boundary and remember to add both directions for return traffic. Third, VPC Endpoints let private resources access supported AWS services without the public internet: use gateway endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB and interface endpoints for PrivateLink services, taking care to update route tables or security groups as required.
